newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya presents budget in "traumatic" conditions.
newsitem.headline: Kenya presents budget in "traumatic" conditions.

text.p: Kenyan Finance Minister Musalia presented his 1997/98 budget to parliament on Thursday in what he called "traumatic conditions" after protests and fisticuffs inside the chamber wrecked his speech.
His speech was inaudible because of the televised pandemonium and Mudavadi warned the opposition of the negative consequences of their protest.
"That type of action can be responsible for capital flight," he told a news conference later. "I have experienced traumatic conditions. What happened in there was very unfortunate."
The budget dwelt on initiatives to improve infrastructure, removal of unecessary regulations to lower the cost of doing business and a lower the tax burden to raise retained earnings.

It also showed that a second cellular phone network would be licensed in Kenya by November and that 30 percent of Telkoms Kenya would be sold to the public through the Nairobi Stock Exchange when Kenya Posts and Telecommunications Corp is split -- sometime in 1998.
The budget also carried further privatisation initiatives for Kenya Railways and the National Cereals and Produce Board.
Mudavadi pledged new anti-dumping and anti-subsidies laws and laws to counter diversion of good in transit to Kenya.

Mudavadi estimated gross total expenditure to reach 192.378 billion shillings ($3.49 billion) in June 1997/July 1998 compared to revenues, including foreign grants, of 185.92 billion. That would result in a budget deficit of around 6.458 billion.
Figures he issued showed gross total expenditure at 180.227 billion shillings in 1996/97 compared to revenues of 169.575 billion shillings, giving a deficit of 10.65 billion.

Earlier figures showed recurrent expenditures for 1996/97 at around 135.214 billion shillings but Mudavadi's financial statement listed that only as current expenditure, before inclusion of development expenditure and a contigency fund.

Mudavadi said drought that swept Kenya in the first quarter of 1997 had severely undermined economic growth and gross domestic product (GDP) growth was now expected at 4.0 percent in 1997 compared to 4.6 percent in 1996 and 4.8 percent in 1995.
He said the drought had led to a dramatic rise in food prices, forcing a rise in inflation to 12.3 percent in the first quarter of 1997 from 5.1 percent in 1995/96.
He raised levies on cigarettes and beer. He also raised the road maintenance levy on petroleum to finance repair of roads.
Mudavadi said that reforms in the last four years had led to Kenya's economic growth and it was the government's desire to follow this growth through despite weather problems.
In a prescient sentence, he said in the prepared speech:
"We should guard against anything that might threaten the macroeconomic stability that has taken us years to achieve. Our utterances and actions should not be for mere political expediency."

Mudavadi said he designed his measures to spur savings and investments, promote industrialisation and create jobs. The speech was drowned out by stamping and shouting from placard-waving opposition MPs who staged an unprecedented protest inside the chamber to press for constitutional reforms.
As President Daniel arap Moi watched, ruling party and opposition members exchanged blows on several occasions.
Mudavadi later told reporters that under Kenyan law the budget must be presented by June 20 and a failure to read it would have led immediately to the dissolution of parliament.
Mudavadi proposed wide-ranging tax rationalisation reforms that he said aimed at reducing the tax burden on individuals and companies and which was designed to encourage tax payments.
Top rate taxes for individuals and corporations came down 2.5 percent to 32.5 percent, Mudavadi said. taxes for foreign-owned corporations eased to 40 from 42.5 percent.
Mudavadi also laid out plans to reform local authorities.
($1=55 shillings).
